title: Methodology
text: The workflow uses a frequentist Network Meta-Analysis framework implemented through the netmeta R package.

title: Methodology
text:
Data structure
The current pipeline expects pairwise contrast data with the following columns:
study, treat1, treat2, logHR, selogHR
Here, logHR is the log hazard ratio and selogHR is its standard error.

title: Methodology
text:
Models
The original Shiny app supports three analysis modes:

Simple treatment-level NMA using netmeta().
Additive Component Network Meta-Analysis using netcomb() or discomb().
Interaction CNMA using a component interaction C-matrix when the network is connected.



Code
source("R/nma_functions.R")
source("R/node_merging.R")

components <- extract_components(dat)
knitr::kable(data.frame(components = components))

title: Methodology
text:
Connectivity logic
For CNMA, the app checks whether the treatment network is connected using igraph. If the network is connected, netcomb() is used. If it is disconnected, discomb() is used. Interaction CNMA is only attempted on connected networks.

title: Limitations and Next Steps
section: What should remain in Shiny or a server-backed app
text:
What should remain in Shiny or a server-backed app

User uploads.
Persistent version history.
REDCap connection.
Saving user-specific analysis states.
Full app-like workflow with sessions and database storage.

title: Limitations and Next Steps
text:
Main technical risk
The main uncertainty for browser-side execution is whether netmeta, its dependencies, and plotting functions run reliably inside webR/WebAssembly. Therefore, the initial Quarto version should be static and reproducible; live browser-side modules should be added only after a minimal netmeta proof of concept succeeds.

title: Living Network Meta-Analysis Tool
text:
Code
source("R/nma_functions.R")
dat <- load_pairwise_data()
This Quarto website is a static, reproducible version of the original Shiny prototype for a Living Network Meta-Analysis workflow. The original app logic has been decomposed into reusable R functions and rendered as an analysis website suitable for GitHub Pages.

title: Living Network Meta-Analysis Tool
text:
Project aim
The aim is to provide a transparent workflow for:

preparing pairwise study-level data,
fitting frequentist Network Meta-Analysis models with netmeta,
exploring treatment networks,
presenting league tables and ranking,
documenting inconsistency checks,
demonstrating node-merging sensitivity analysis.

title: Inconsistency
text:
Code
source("R/nma_functions.R")
dat <- load_pairwise_data()
nm <- run_model(dat, model_type = "simple", effect_model = "random")

title: Inconsistency
text:
Local inconsistency: node-splitting


Code
ns <- tryCatch(
  netmeta::netsplit(
    nm,
    random = TRUE,
    common = FALSE,
    backtransf = TRUE
  ),
  error = identity
)

if (inherits(ns, "error")) {
  cat("Node-splitting failed:", conditionMessage(ns))
} else {

  dir <- ns$direct.random[, c("comparison", "TE", "lower", "upper", "p")]
  ind <- ns$indirect.random[, c("comparison", "TE", "lower", "upper", "p")]
  cmp <- ns$compare.random[, c("comparison", "z", "p")]

  res <- merge(
    dir,
    ind,
    by = "comparison",
    all = TRUE,
    suffixes = c(".direct", ".indirect")
  )

  res <- merge(
    res,
    cmp,
    by = "comparison",
    all = TRUE
  )

  res$Q <- res$z^2
  res$df <- 1L

  names(res)[names(res) == "TE.direct"] <- "Direct"
  names(res)[names(res) == "TE.indirect"] <- "Indirect"
  names(res)[names(res) == "p.x"] <- "p.direct"
  names(res)[names(res) == "p.y"] <- "p.indirect"
  names(res)[names(res) == "p"] <- "p.diff"

  out <- res[, c(
    "comparison",
    "Direct",
    "Indirect",
    "lower.direct",
    "upper.direct",
    "lower.indirect",
    "upper.indirect",
    "z",
    "Q",
    "df",
    "p.diff"
  )]

  numcols <- c(
    "Direct",
    "Indirect",
    "lower.direct",
    "upper.direct",
    "lower.indirect",
    "upper.indirect",
    "z",
    "Q",
    "p.diff"
  )

  out[numcols] <- lapply(
    out[numcols],
    function(x) if (is.numeric(x)) round(x, 3) else x
  )

  out <- out[order(out$comparison), ]

  knitr::kable(
    out,
    caption = "Node-splitting results: direct, indirect, and direct-versus-indirect evidence"
  )
}

title: Interactive Node Merging
text: This page provides a browser-side node-merging module for the example CLL network. The user selects the treatment components to merge, gives the merged node a new name, chooses the CNMA model, and presses Run node merging. The code is hidden from the user; only the controls, network plot, and results are shown.

title: Interactive Node Merging
text:
Notes for thesis interpretation
This is a client-side sensitivity module. It allows users to perform controlled node merging on the embedded example dataset, but it does not save choices to a database and does not create a permanent version history. For a full Living NMA platform with uploaded datasets, persistent versions, and user sessions, the Shiny/server version remains the correct production architecture.

title: Live Demo Roadmap
text:
This page is reserved for the browser-side version of selected modules.
The safest development order is:

title: Live Demo Roadmap
text:
Minimal test code for quarto-live/webR
Use this only after adding the quarto-live extension to the project.
install.packages("netmeta")
library(netmeta)

example_dat <- data.frame(
  studlab = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  treat1 = c("A", "B", "A"),
  treat2 = c("B", "C", "C"),
  TE = c(0.20, -0.10, 0.05),
  seTE = c(0.12, 0.15, 0.10)
)

net <- netmeta(
  TE = TE,
  seTE = seTE,
  treat1 = treat1,
  treat2 = treat2,
  studlab = studlab,
  data = example_dat,
  sm = "HR",
  random = TRUE
)

summary(net)
If this works in the browser, then the node-merging demo can be made genuinely live. If it fails, use precomputed node-merging scenarios in the static Quarto website.
